title: LiDAR: A Spinning Laser
description: Component lesson. Take the ultrasonic sensor's whole idea, swap sound for light, and spin it in a circle. The room appears out of nothing.

content.value: An ultrasonic sensor gives you one distance reading, in the direction it's pointed. LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) asks the exact same question — how far away is something? — but spins a laser around in a full circle, taking a fresh reading at every angle, building up a complete picture of everything around the robot instead of just what's straight ahead.

The core measurement is identical to ultrasonic's: send a pulse, time how long it takes to come back, compute distance. LiDAR just uses light instead of sound — much faster, so the timing has to be measured in nanoseconds rather than milliseconds — and it does that measurement over and over while spinning, once per degree or better.

content.title: 🔦 Watch it sweep
content.hint: Follow the red ray around. Each dot it drops stays put — watch the room's shape build up from nothing.

content.value: After a full rotation, those individual dots — a point cloud — trace out the shape of everything around the sensor: walls, furniture, other robots. That's a complete local map, rebuilt fresh every rotation, which is exactly what lets a robot navigate a room it's never seen before.
You'll compare LiDAR head-to-head against ultrasonic in the next lesson — same basic idea, very different trade-offs in cost, resolution, and what kinds of surfaces trip each one up.

Key takeaway: LiDAR is the same time-of-flight idea as an ultrasonic sensor, using light instead of sound, spun through a full circle to build a complete map of the surroundings rather than one single-direction reading.

quiz.question: What's the core measurement LiDAR shares with an ultrasonic sensor?
options: Distance from a round-trip time of flight
quiz.explain: Both work the same way at heart: send a pulse, time its return, compute distance — light instead of sound is the only real difference.

quiz.question: What does one full LiDAR rotation give you that a single ultrasonic sensor can't?
options: A reading in every direction at once, building a complete map rather than one direction's distance
quiz.explain: Spinning through 360° and taking a reading at each angle produces a full point cloud of the surroundings, not just one straight-ahead number.

quiz.question: Why does LiDAR need to measure time in nanoseconds instead of the milliseconds an ultrasonic sensor uses?
options: Light travels vastly faster than sound, so its round trip takes far less time to measure
It's an arbitrary design choice with no physical reason
LiDAR doesn't actually measure time at all
quiz.explain: Light's speed is about a million times sound's — the same round-trip idea just happens on a vastly shorter timescale.
